analysis.title: Active Diversification: Mitigating Collective Risks
key_insights: Invesco argues that cap-weighted passive index strategies now carry 'collective risk': rising concentration, shared exposures and price-agnostic flows tie risk to investor behavior rather than security fundamentals. It proposes 'active diversification', the intentional use of active strategies to diversify away from market-embedded preferences.

The Magnificent Seven (GOOGL, AMZN, AAPL, META, MSFT, NVDA, TSLA) made up over 30% of the S&P 500 at the end of January 2026. The S&P 500 effective number of constituents (ENC) fell to roughly 43 stocks, against a 1990-2026 average of 112 and about one-third of the long-term average.

Collective risk differs from endogenous risk. Endogenous risk is episodic, tied to a specific strategy and needs a trigger (Black Monday 1987, a 22.6% one-day fall; the 2007 quant crisis). Collective risk accumulates continuously from shared ownership and flows, and is the condition that makes an unwind possible.

Lochstoer and Muir (2026) estimate daily market volatility is up about 127% since the mid-1950s, with index-based trading coinciding with higher volatility and comovement. Green, Krishnan and Sturm (2026) model that volatility could rise sharply if passive ownership goes from about 50% to roughly 65%.

Kritzman and Turkington (2026) argue current concentration has historical precedent and little predictive power for returns. Clarke, de Silva and Thorley (2026) counter with a volatility-weighted ENC: the largest constituents now combine high index weights with above-median realized volatility, the first sustained episode of that in a century, and the pattern appears across major global markets.

Equal weighting is the simplest ('uninformed') diversifier. A 43% allocation to an equal-weighted S&P 500 portfolio restores the combined ENC to the historical average of 112. Equal weighting introduces a size bias and generally outperforms cap-weighted except when index concentration is high.

Preference-factor test on S&P 500 stocks: annualized returns for 1970-2024 were 11.0% (S&P 500), 11.1% (High Preference), 13.7% (Medium) and 14.6% (Low). For 2000-2024 they were 7.7%, 6.6%, 11.0% and 13.6%. Average correlation with the S&P 500 was 0.96 (High), 0.93 (Medium) and 0.84 (Low).

Stock-selection models (Guerard et al.) add information in layers: fundamentals, then earnings forecasts, then momentum. Information coefficients rise from 0.02 to 0.03, 0.04 and 0.05 across four model specifications over 1980-2020 US data. Adding forecasts, revisions and breadth improves quintile returns and spreads in all segments. Momentum helps in most markets but hurts US large cap.

Active opportunity is strongest where information dispersion is high and passive ownership is lower: emerging markets (Model 3 Q1-Q5 spread 14.0%, information ratio 1.08), developed markets ex-US (9.9%, 0.79) and US small/mid cap (8.8%, 0.36). US large cap shows muted gains (Model 3 spread 3.9%, information ratio 0.12).

Three implementation principles: (1) allow flexibility to differ from the market by merging narrow size/region/style silos into broader exposures; (2) diversify information sources by combining quantitative and fundamental strategies, sized meaningfully against a tracking-error budget; (3) allocate for risk mitigation where passive ownership and concentration are highest (equal-weight, quant) and for return enhancement where dispersion is greatest (fundamental).

Clarke, de Silva and Thorley estimate that, because underweighting large volatile constituents uses up tracking-error budget faster, some benchmark-relative managers may have roughly a third less deployable active risk than in the 2010s.

Economic policy uncertainty indexes for the world, US, Europe, UK and China have trended higher since 1998, with larger and more frequent spikes. Invesco says this is the environment in which collective risk is most dangerous.
risk_factors: Concentration in a few mega-cap names and rising passive ownership could amplify volatility and weaken price discovery.
Rising economic policy uncertainty widens the range of outcomes while shared positioning narrows the risks a portfolio actually diversifies against.
Active diversification carries wider relative performance outcomes ('wrong and alone'), implementation frictions (fees, capacity) and the risk of abandoning strategies during underperformance.
Equal-weighted strategies introduce a size bias and tend to lag cap-weighted indexes when index concentration is high.
Quant models rely on measurable risk and may fail where uncertainty is unmeasurable. Momentum detracted from US large-cap results.
charts_described: Exhibit 2 plots the S&P 500 effective number of constituents from 1990 to 2026: average ENC of 112, current level 43.
Exhibit 3 shows the ENC of an S&P 500 holding rising with the share in an equal-weighted portfolio, reaching the 112 average at a 43% allocation.
Exhibit 5 Panel A shows annualized returns for the S&P 500 and High/Medium/Low Preference portfolios for 1970-2024 (11.0%, 11.1%, 13.7%, 14.6%) and 2000-2024 (7.7%, 6.6%, 11.0%, 13.6%).

Exhibit 7 reports quintile returns, Q1-Q5 spreads, Sharpe and information ratios for three stock-selection models across World, Developed ex-US, Emerging Markets, US, US Large Cap and US Small-Mid Cap, 2005-2025.
vol_and_positioning: Passive ownership of US equities is currently about 50% (per Green, Krishnan and Sturm), and a rise to roughly 65% could sharply increase volatility in their model.
S&P 500 ENC is roughly 43 constituents, with the Magnificent Seven at over 30% of the index as of end-January 2026.
Lochstoer and Muir (2026) estimate daily market volatility has risen about 127% since the mid-1950s, with higher stock comovement and a larger share of returns driven by common factors.
Clarke, de Silva and Thorley find the largest index constituents combine high weights with above-median realized volatility, so risk is concentrated in fewer names than capital weights imply.

tension_points.bull_case: Kritzman and Turkington (2026) argue today's concentration has historical precedent, has little predictive power for future returns, and is less concerning because the largest companies are often more diversified and less volatile.
tension_points.bear_case: Clarke, de Silva and Thorley (2026) show the largest constituents now combine high index weights with above-median realized volatility, concentrating risk in fewer names than capital weights imply, across major global markets.
